workEn: The Secret History of the Mongols
title: 元朝秘史 §§125–130
titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §§125–130: Chinggis Qan's Thanks, the Kereid Compact, and Jamuqa's Desertions
part: §§125–130 — Chinggis Qan's Thanks, the Kereid Compact, and Jamuqa's Desertions
source: Mongγol-un niγuča tobčiyan (The Secret History of the Mongols), §§125–130, in the Ming Chinese-character phonetic transcription, as edited with a romanized reading by Shiratori Kurakichi 白鳥庫吉, 音訳蒙文元朝秘史 (Tokyo, 1943), itself based on the Ye Dehui 葉德輝 printed edition of 1905/1908; text taken from the Japanese Wikisource transcription, archived and verified against it character for character. Shiratori died in 1942, so the edition was public domain in Japan before the URAA date and was never restored in the United States. Section numbering (§) is the standard citation system. Romanization convention: Shiratori's, kept exactly as he prints it (γ, ġ, ṅ, ž, č, and the raised dot of γ̇). Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian, with the Ming interlinear Chinese glosses as the primary crib. No modern translation was consulted. langCode is null: there is no text-to-speech for Middle Mongol.
about: Six sections. §125 has Chinggis, now Qan, thank Bo'orchu and Jelme for their company and set them over the rest. §126 sends Daqai and Sükegei to To'oril Qan of the Kereid, whose answer is that Temüjin should be Qan and that the compact must not be broken. §127 tells how Chinggis sends Arqai-Qasar and Cha'urqan to Jamuqa, who answers with a message for Altan and Quchar, who had made Chinggis Qan and parted Jamuqa from his anda. §128 tells how Jamuqa's younger brother Taichar took Jüchi-Darmala's herd and was shot dead for it. §129 follows the war: Jamuqa and the thirteen Jadaran come, Chinggis meets them at Dalan-Baljut and falls back to the Cherene gorge, and Jamuqa boils the Chinos princes. §130 tells how the Uruqud and Mongqud and Father Münlig leave Jamuqa for Chinggis, and how a feast on the Onon ends with a beaten cook. The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting.

sentences.l: There Čiṅgis Qaγan Qan becoming, Boγ̇orču, Želme two-to on-speaking:
sentences.i: There Chinggis Qahan, now Qan, said to Bo'orchu and Jelme, the two of them:
sentences.n: Tende Čiṅgis Qaγan qān bolžu is 'there Chinggis Qahan, becoming qan' (Ming 做着, the converb): the Qan now speaks as Qan. qojar-a (Ming 兩箇行) is 'to the two', summing up the pair named before it; the comma after Boγ̇orču is Shiratori's. Shiratori's quotation mark opens on the next word and runs on to the end of the section's speech.

morph.gloss: me (bi 'I', oblique stem nama-) [我 行]
accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)

sentences.l: You two me-(acc.) shadow-than other companion without-when, shadow becoming, heart my set-at-rest, indeed you;
sentences.i: "You two set my heart at rest, becoming my shadow when I had no companion but my shadow;
sentences.n: Ta qojar nama-ji is 'you two, me': the Ming 我行 marks nama-ji as an object, but the verb takes sedkil min-u 'my heart' as its object, so nama-ji is probably 'for me'. seġüder-eče busu nökör ügei-dür is 'when there was no companion other than the shadow' (Ming 除影兒別伴當無時): the ablative -eče does the work of 'than', and ügei-dür is 'in the absence of'. amuγ̇ulba is amu- 'peace' + causative -γ̇ul- + -ba, 'caused to be at peace' (Ming 敎安了); the stem is inferred. že ta, 'indeed, you', closes the clause. The grammar of the first half is clear; the sense of 'becoming a shadow' (Ming 影兒做着) is a figure, I take it, for sticking close beside him.

sentences.t: sedkil-dür atuγai" keġebe.

morph.gloss: optative, third person: 'let it be, may it ...'

sentences.l: Heart-in let-it-remain" he-said.
sentences.i: Keep it in your hearts," he said.
sentences.n: atuγai is a- 'be, remain' with the optative -tuγai: 'let it remain' (Ming 存者). Whose heart it is, the Ming does not say: sedkil-dür follows ta; and so I read 'in your heart', the heart of the two being addressed. The closing mark after atuγai and the stop after keġebe are Shiratori's; the next speech begins with a new opening mark.

morph.gloss: without, there is not [無 時]

sentences.l: "Tail-than other whip without-when, tail becoming, heart my set-at-rest, indeed you;
sentences.i: "You set my heart at rest, becoming my tail when I had no whip but a tail;
sentences.n: The speech repeats the first with a different figure: seġül-eče busu čičuγ̇a ügei-dür is 'when there was no whip other than the tail' (Ming 尾子處別鞭子無時), and seġül bolžu 'becoming the tail'. The Ming 尾子 'tail' is not explained, and what a horse's or a man's tail stands for as a whip (a following, or the thing behind him) I cannot say; I give the words and do not guess. žirüge is a second word for 'heart', beside sedkil; the Ming 心 glosses both alike.

sentences.t: čeġeži dotora min-u atuγai" keġebe.

morph.gloss: genitive ending, set after its noun
optative, third person: 'let it be, may it ...'

sentences.l: Breast inside my let-it-remain" he-said.
sentences.i: Keep it within my own breast," he said.
sentences.n: čeġeži dotora min-u atuγai: 'breast within my let-it-remain' (Ming 胷懷內我的敎存者). The Ming reads it as 'let it remain within my breast'; whether the speaker asks them to keep his words, or to let their service remain with him, the line does not say. I give 'keep it' as a plain reading.

sentences.t: "Ta qojar urida baiγsaγ̇ar ede bükün-i aqalažu ülü-ü aqun ta" keġebe.

morph.gloss: to stand, to be set up (stem inferred from the Ming 立) [立了的上頭]
past participle -γsan with instrumental -ar: 'because of having ...ed' (the Ming 上頭 'on account of'; the split of the ending is uncertain)
all, those who are (from bü- 'to be'; Ming 有的 'those existing') [有的 行]
makes a verb from a noun: to act as, to do with ...
particle of question (uncertain; the Ming puts its 麽 on the next word)
ending of the verb (uncertain; the Ming 住麽 reads it as a question, 'will you dwell?')

sentences.l: "You two earlier because-of-having-stood these existing-ones elder-being not-? dwell you," he-said.
sentences.i: "Since you two stood first, will you not stay as elders over all of these?" he said.
sentences.n: baiγsaγ̇ar is bai- 'stand, be set up' + past participle -γsan + instrumental -ar, 'because of having stood' (Ming 立了的上頭 'on account of having stood'): they stood first. ede bükün-i is 'these, all who are' (Ming 這的每有的行). aqalažu is aqa 'elder' + -la- + -žu, 'being elder, taking the place of the elder' (Ming 爲長着). ülü-ü aqun ta: ülü 'not', -ü perhaps the question particle, aqun 'dwell, stay'; the Ming 不住麽 asks 'will you not stay?'. The ending of aqun is not settled (see also in §126). The sense is the appointment of the two as chiefs over the rest; it does not say of what they are made elders.

sentences.i: Chinggis Qahan spoke again:
sentences.n: basa 'again' (Ming 再) shows a second speech of the Qan. Shiratori's quotation mark opens on the next word and runs to the end of the section.

sentences.t: Teṅgiri γažar-a küčü nemežü igeġegdeġesü

morph.gloss: Heaven, Tengri (the sky as a god) [天]
to protect, to help (stem inferred from the Ming 護助) [被護助呵]

sentences.l: "Heaven Earth-to strength adding, if-it-be-protected,
sentences.i: "If Heaven and Earth add strength to us, and we are protected,
sentences.n: Teṅgiri γažar-a küčü nemežü is 'Heaven, to the Earth, adding strength' (Ming 天地行氣力添着). The -a on γažar-a is 'to', as the Ming 行 marks, and so the line reads 'Heaven adds strength to the Earth'; I take the pair as one force that gives strength, and I read 'to us' in order to make a sense; the Ming has no 'us'. igeġegdeġesü is a passive of a stem igeġe- (inferred from the Ming 護助 'protect, help') with the conditional -ġesü: 'if it is protected'.

sentences.t: ta Žamuqa anda-ača nama-ji keġen sedkižü nököčešü keġen

morph.gloss: Jamuqa, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
sworn brother, pledged friend (Ming 契合) [(契合)處]
accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)
to be a companion (from nökör; stem inferred) [做伴我]
ending of exhortation, 'let ...' (uncertain; the Ming 做伴我 'be a companion to me')

sentences.l: you Žamuqa anda-from me-(acc.) saying, thinking, 'let-them-be-companion-to-me' saying
sentences.i: you, thinking of me, saying 'let them be my companions' from Jamuqa the anda,
sentences.n: A hard line. Ming: 您人名契合處我行麽道想着做伴我麽道: 'you, from Jamuqa the anda, saying ‘to me’, thinking, saying ‘be companions to me’'. I read ta ... sedkižü nököčešü keġen as 'you, thinking ‘let them be companions to me’', with the speech or thought of the two men. nököčešü is nököče- 'be a companion' with an ending -šü that I take as a hortative from the Ming 做伴我; this ending is uncertain. The place of Jamuqa anda-ača is uncertain: either the people come from Jamuqa, or the thought is about Jamuqa. I leave the grammar as given and say that the line is not yet clear to me.

sentences.l: come-ones old-men blessed companions my not-? become you," he-said.
sentences.i: the old men who came, blessed, my companions: will they not be mine, you?" he said.
sentences.n: iregsed ötögüs ölže- ten nököd min-u: 'the ones who came, the old men, the blessed (ölže + -ten 'having blessing'; Shiratori's line break splits the word), companions of mine'. boluγ̇užai ends in a form I cannot name; the Ming 不做麽 (not-become?) asks a question, so 'will they not become ...?'. I take it as 'my companions', and the speech as an appeal: those who came are mine, so you two, take them up. The sense of the whole speech from 'If Heaven and Earth' on is uncertain and I mark it so.

sentences.t: "Žüg žüg tüšibe tan-i."

morph.gloss: to entrust, to commit to (Ming 委付) [委付了]
you (stem of ta before a case ending) [您行]

sentences.l: "Each each entrusted you."
sentences.i: "I have entrusted you, each to his own place."
sentences.n: žüg žüg is 'each, each' (Ming 各各), žüg being 'side, direction'. tüšibe is tüši- 'entrust' (Ming 委付) in the past, and tan-i is 'you (acc.)'. The stem tüši- is attested here for the first time in the work. Whether it means 'put in charge' or 'rely on' is not settled; the Ming's 委付 is 'entrust'. The mark closes the speech and the section's long quotation.

sentences.t: Čiṅgis Qaγan-(n)i qān bolγaba.

morph.gloss: Chinggis, a man's name (personal name; the name taken by Temüjin) [太祖︀]

sentences.i: They made Chinggis Qahan Qan.
sentences.n: bolγaba is bol- 'become' + causative -γa- + -ba, 'made to become' (Ming 敎做了). The subject is not stated. The stop after bolγaba is Shiratori's; keġen in the next unit takes the sentence up as a quotation.

morph.gloss: the Kereid, a people (the -d is probably plural) [種名(的)]

sentences.l: saying, the Kereid's Toγ̇oril Qān-to, Daγai, Sükegei two-(acc.) envoys he-sent.
sentences.i: Saying so, he sent Daqai and Sükegei as envoys to To'oril Qan of the Kereid.
sentences.n: keġen is keġe- 'say' + -n, 'saying' (Ming 麽道), the quotation marker that closes the speech. The envoys go to To'oril Qan: Kereid-ün Toγ̇oril Qān-dur 'the Kereid's To'oril Qan-to'. qojar-i 'the two' (Ming 兩箇行) is an accusative, 'sent the two as envoys'. ilebe is ile- (Ming 去了 'went') in the past; with elči 'envoy' and the accusative on the men I read 'sent'. Daγai is printed with D here; the four envoys of §124 include a Taγai, probably the same man, and i spells each as printed.

sentences.l: Toγ̇oril Qān Temüžin the son-(acc.) my Qan to-be-made na right.
sentences.i: To'oril Qan said: "That Temüjin, my son, be made Qan: that is right.
sentences.n: No speech verb stands here, but the Ming gives no sign of a break: To'oril Qan answers the envoys; the word 'said' and the opening mark in i are mine. köġün-i 'the son' (Ming 兒子行) is accusative, with Temüžin köġün-i as the object of bolγaqu, the future participle of the causative bol-γa-, 'to be made'. na is a particle for which the Ming has 好生 'good, well'; I do not know its force. žöb is 'right' (Ming 是). Shiratori has no opening mark here; the closing mark falls at the end of the speech after tamtuludqun.

sentences.t: Monγol qā ügeġün ker aqun ta.

morph.gloss: qa'an, sovereign (a short form of qaγan) [皇帝]
plural, 'those' (uncertain; the Ming 每 marks a plural)

sentences.i: How would you Mongols stay without a Qahan?
sentences.n: qā is a contracted form of qaγan (its plural is qād, 'sovereigns', elsewhere in the glossary); I give it the house 'Qahan'. The Ming glosses 皇帝 again. ügeġün: ügei 'without' with an ending -ġün that the Ming's 每 shows to be a plural, 'the ones without a qa'an'. ker aqun ta 'how will you stay'; again aqun, now with the Ming 過的 'pass the time'.

prohibitive/imperative, second person plural (uncertain; the Ming 您 'you')

sentences.i: Do not break this compact of yours;

sentences.i: do not undo the bond of the compact;
sentences.n: žaṅgi is 'bond, knot' (Ming 結了的 'tied'); -ban is reflexive. taludqun is talu- 'untie, undo' (the stem is inferred from the Ming 解了) with the same plural prohibitive ending as the line before.

sentences.t: žaqa-ban bu tamtuludqun" keġežü iležü.

morph.gloss: collar (Ming 衣領) [衣領 自的行]
to tear (stem inferred from the Ming 扯) [扯了您]

sentences.l: collar-one's-own do-not you-tear" saying he-sent.
sentences.i: do not tear the collar," he said, and sent them off.
sentences.n: žaqa-ban is 'one's own collar' (Ming 衣領). tamtuludqun is tamtulu- 'tear off' (stem inferred from the Ming 扯了) plus the same ending. The three prohibitions are a figure: a compact is a knot, a collar. keġežü iležü: 'saying, going/sending'; the Ming glosses iležü 去着 'going', and I take it as To'oril sending the envoys on their way.

sentences.i: When he sent Arqai-Qasar and Cha'urqan to Jamuqa as envoys,
sentences.n: A converb chain starts here and goes on to the end of the speech: ileġesü is ile- 'send' + conditional -ġesü (Ming 去呵), 'when/if (he) sent'; qojar-i is the accusative object, so the verb is active, as in ilebe of §126. Arγai-Qasar is printed as one name with a hyphen, as in the prior part; the Ming glosses 人名 for both. The sentence has no stated subject.

sentences.t: "Altan, Qučar qojar-a ügüle" keġen ügüležü ilerün;

morph.gloss: Altan, a man's name (personal name; the word means 'gold') [人名]
Quchar, a man's name (personal name) [人名]
to speak, to say (here the bare stem, imperative: 'say!') [說]

sentences.l: "Altan, Qučar two-to say" saying speaking on-sending;
sentences.i: "Say it to Altan and Quchar, the two," and, so saying, sending them off,
sentences.n: A message within a message. ügüle is the bare stem, an imperative 'say' (Ming 說); keġen ügüležü is 'saying, speaking': two converbs for one act, the second repeating the first. ilerün is ile- 'send' + -rün, 'on sending/going' (Ming 去). The Ming does not say whether Jamuqa speaks to the envoys or the envoys to Altan and Quchar.

sentences.l: "Altan, Qučar, you two Temüžin anda we two between anda's
sentences.i: "Altan and Quchar, you two, between us two, Temüjin the anda and me, the anda's
sentences.n: A direct address to Altan and Quchar (Ming 您兩箇). ba qojar is 'we two' (Ming 俺兩箇), so Temüžin anda ba qojar is 'Temüjin the anda and I, we two' (compare Anda ba qojar-i in the next unit); žaγ̇ura 'between' (Ming 間). Anda-jin is 'of the anda' (Ming 契合的), with a capital A in Shiratori's print. Shiratori puts a comma after Altan and a second after Qučar; it is not clear whether the anda-bond belongs to Temüjin or to both.

sentences.n: qariγuluγ̇ad is qari- 'return' + causative -γul- + -γ̇ad, 'having caused to turn back' (Ming 敎囘了), with Žamuqa-ji 'Jamuqa (acc.)' (Ming 行) as its object. Žamuqa-ji is an accusative, so the clause is 'having made Jamuqa turn back, having sent Jamuqa back' (Ming 敎囘了, as qariγuluγ̇ad in the glossary), and I keep that. Who does it is not stated; the next lines tell of men leaving Jamuqa, and 'turning back from Jamuqa' would be a reading of them, not of this word. tendēče is tende 'there' + -ēče with a long ē, which Shiratori prints.
